newsitem.title: SPAIN: Latam boom boosts Telefonica's attraction.
newsitem.headline: Latam boom boosts Telefonica's attraction.

text.p: It was a gamble that seems to have paid off for Telefonica de Espana: the company's heavy investment in uncharted Latin American markets has attracted powerful suitors who now want a piece of the action.

U.S. telecoms operators MCI and AT&T are locked in intense competition for an alliance with Spain's former state telephone monopoly, a deal they hope will give them a ticket to Latin America's fast-growing telecoms business.

Portugal Telecom accidentally tipped MCI as the likely winner in an announcement about its own alliance with MCI and British Telecom on Monday, but Telefonica quickly denied a deal had been reached and said it was still in talks with AT&T as well as with MCI/BT.

Telefonica, which has in the last decade built itself into Latin America's biggest foreign telecoms provider, has also been courted by GTE, SBC Communications, and Bell Atlantic, company officials said last month.
The "jewel in our crown", as Telefonica chairman Juan Villalonga put it, is the company's international subsidiary TISA, which has a dominant presence in Peru, Chile, Venezuela, and Argentina.
Telefonica Internacional SA-TISA also has solid positions in Brazil, Colombia, Puerto Rico and Romania and a foothold in the United States and Portugal.
The group's aggressive campaign to become the leading Latin American operator started in the early 1990s as a response to the threat of competition in its domestic market.
At the time, the region's economies were far from stable and TISA's strategic purchase of former state operators as they came to market looked like a risky gamble.

When TISA bought control of the two Peruvian phone companies CTP-Peru and Entel in March 1994, it was for an unheard-of $2 billion, far above the next highest bidder, and caused Moody's rating agency to downgrade its short-term debt.
Telefonica contested the downgrade and defended the purchase, whose high price unsettled markets, as vital for getting a dominant position in the Latin American market.
Company officials at the time said Telefonica was determined to shut out its big U.S. competitors, the same operators who are now vying for a partnership with it.
The gamble appears to have paid off.
While only 15 percent of Telefonica's earnings come from TISA, of which it owns 76 percent with the other 24 percent still state owned, the subsidiary has big growth potential.

Latin America has emerged from recession far faster than expected with growth of more than three percent in 1996, well above the 1995 crisis level of less than one percent, the Inter-American Development Bank said last month.

The shares of Latin American telephone companies began surging on Wall Street early in the year as investors, who fled the region's markets after Mexico's fiscal collapse in late 1994, returned in force.
Analysts said the region's growth rate, coupled with the enormous room for expansion in the under-served market, made stocks in Latin American telecoms seem under-priced.
Telefonica, which now calls itself the "undisputed leader in the Spanish-speaking world", had sales last year through TISA of some 350 billion pesetas ($2.4 million).
TISA participates in the management of some 10 million telephone lines, with some 965,000 mobile phone, 1.1 million cable television and 130,000 bleeper clients.

Its major holdings are 35 percent of CPT-Telefonica del Peru SA, 43.62 percent of Compania de Telecommunicaciones de Chile-CTC, 18.66 percent of Telefonica de Argentina SA-TASA, 4.88 percent of Compania Anonima de Telefonos de Venezuela-CANTV and 79 percent of Telefonica Larga Distancia de Puerto Rico-TLD.
Telefonica also participated in a consortium that won 35 percent of the Brazilian operator Companhia Riograndense de Telecomunicacoes-CRT.
